The lateral pain system, which includes the lateral thalamic nuclei and the anterior cingulate cortex and insula, is responsible for sensory/ discriminative aspects of pain. Therefore, the patient will be able to recognise where the stimulus has been applied, what the stimulus has been (i.e. pressure) and the intensity of the stimulus. However, the medial pain system which includes the medial thalamic nuclei and the other primary affective/cognitive pain system is responsible for the emotional/ cognitive aspects of pain. Therefore, the patient will not experience as much emotional/ cognitive pain from the stimulus.  The fact that the lesions are in the left S1 and S2 cortices means there is a contralateral effect i.e. less sensory/ emotional pain from the right side of the body. This is because the majority of the fibre entering the spinal tract crosses over in the spinal cord before ascending to the left S1 and S2.

When the complement component C3 is cleaved by C3 convertase, it produces both C3a and C3b. C3a contributes to deactivation of the activated  (iC3b) by forming a stable non-regulatory complex. C3b binds to and coats antigens on microorganisms in a process called opsonisation, making them more palatable for phagocytosis by phagocytes. C3b also binds to and activates J-related protein (CR1) on neutrophils and macrophages, enhancing their phagocytic capacity. C3a and C5a are both anaphylatoxins which induce degranulation of basophils and mast cells, leading to the release of histamine. This causes inflammation of the site, with histamine increasing vascular permeability and causing vasodilation. C3a and C5a are also chemotaxins, attracting neutrophils and macrophages to the site of infection. C5b binds to and activates the complement receptors CD1, CD3 and CD4 on neutrophils and macrophages, leading to enhanced phagocytosis. C3b and C5b combine to form the membrane attack complex, which inserts into the cell membrane and destroys the cell.

D is correct well done!Once a pathogen has entered the body, the activation of the innate immune system is initiated. One of the cells involved in this is the mast cell. Mast cells release a number of chemicals that have an effect on the surrounding area. One of these effects is inflammation of the area, which is important to stop the spread of the pathogen. One of the chemicals released by mast cells is histamine, which causes vasodilation of vessel walls and makes vessels more permeable. This allows for leukocytes to enter the surrounding tissue and phagocytose the pathogen. Other chemicals released by mast cells include: Eosinophil chemotactic factors (attract eosinophils to the site of infection)ProteasesPecolysins (break down extracellular matrix stores)Serine lipasesChemokines (that draw neutrophils to the site of infection)Nitric oxide (gas produced that inhibits platelet aggregation)Erythrottapeases (activate smooth muscle proteins causing muscle relaxation to reduce blood pressure)Prostaglandins (cause vasodilation, increase vascular permeability and sensitise nociceptors so the area is more painful)So...In summary, mast cells release histamine, causing vasodilation and increased vascular permeability, as well as various other chemicals including eosinophil chemotactic factors, neutrophil chemotactic factors, proteases, etc. These work together to cause inflammation of the area, which allows for leukocytes to enter the area and phagocytose the pathogen.
